# How computers & operating systems work {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## The three things that matter most

::: incremental
-   **CPU** — does the work. Made of **cores** (independent workers) and runs at some **clock speed** (GHz). More cores = more tasks at once.
-   **RAM** — fast, *volatile* working memory. Your data must fit here while you analyze it. **Lost when power is off.**
-   **Disk** — slow, *persistent* storage. SSDs are fast (~0.1 ms); spinning HDDs are slow (~10 ms) but cheap and large.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
The #1 single-cell bottleneck is **RAM**: a big count matrix must fit in memory. "Out of memory" usually means *get more RAM*, not a faster CPU.
:::

## CPU vs GPU (one slide)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**CPU**

-   A few powerful cores (4–64)
-   Great at sequential, branching logic
-   Runs your OS and most R/Bioconductor code
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**GPU**

-   Thousands of small cores
-   Massive parallelism
-   Machine learning, some scRNA-seq tools
:::
:::::

::: {.callout-note}
Most of this workshop runs on the **CPU**. GPUs matter for deep-learning steps and a few accelerated tools.
:::

## What an operating system does

::: incremental
-   The OS is the **manager** sitting between you and the hardware.
-   **Process management** — schedules many running programs across cores.
-   **Memory management** — hands out RAM, protects programs from each other.
-   **File system** — organizes files into directories with permissions.
-   **Security** — users, groups, and the *least-privilege* principle.
:::

## The filesystem & processes

::: incremental
-   Files live in a **tree** of directories; you navigate with paths (`/home/you/data`).
-   A **process** is a running program; the OS gives each a slice of CPU time and a chunk of RAM.
-   On a shared machine, *many users' processes coexist* — so being a good citizen matters (especially on a cluster).
-   Unix/Linux is the lingua franca of scientific computing — the same commands work on your laptop and on Talapas.
:::

# What is an HPC cluster? {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## A cluster, in one picture

::: incremental
-   A **cluster** is many computers ("nodes") wired together to act as one big system.
-   **Login (head) node** — where you land; for light work only (editing, submitting jobs).
-   **Compute nodes** — the workhorses where your jobs actually run.
-   **Shared storage** — a parallel filesystem every node can see.
-   **Scheduler** (SLURM) — decides whose job runs where and when.
:::

## When do you actually need one?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Laptop is fine when...**

-   Data fits in your RAM
-   One sample / small dataset
-   Quick exploration & plotting
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Reach for HPC when...**

-   Data exceeds laptop RAM (many samples)
-   Long-running jobs (hours/days)
-   Many jobs in parallel
-   You need GPUs or huge memory nodes
:::
:::::

::: {.callout-tip}
Rule of thumb: prototype small on your laptop, then scale the *same* workflow up on Talapas.
:::

# UO Talapas {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Meet Talapas

::: incremental
-   UO's flagship HPC cluster, run by **Research Advanced Computing Services (RACS)**.
-   Named from the Chinook word for *coyote* — educator and keeper of knowledge.
-   Scale: **~14,500 CPU cores, 129 TB RAM, ~89 GPUs (A40–H100), ~3 PB storage.**
-   Docs: [Talapas Knowledge Base](https://uoracs.github.io/talapas2-knowledge-base/).
:::

## Getting access: a PIRG + an account

::: incremental
-   Access is tied to a **PIRG** (Principal Investigator Research Group).
-   Ask your **PI** to add you, or have RACS create a new PIRG.
-   Request access at [racs.uoregon.edu/request-access](https://racs.uoregon.edu/request-access).
-   Your **username = your Duck ID**; your **password = your UO password**.
:::

## Logging in: SSH + Duo

``` bash
# Connect with SSH (off campus: connect to UO VPN first)
ssh yourduckid@login.talapas.uoregon.edu
```

::: incremental
-   No characters appear while you type your password — that's normal.
-   Logins require **Duo** two-factor: type `1` and Enter for a push.
-   You land on a **login node** — light tasks only. Heavy jobs there get killed.
:::

## File systems: where things go

| Location | Quota | Purpose |
|--------------------------|-----------|------------------------------------|
| `/home/<duckid>` | 250 GB | Config files, scripts, small installs |
| `/projects/<PIRG>` | 2 TB | Shared project data & analysis |
| `/scratch/<PIRG>` | 20 TB | High-throughput working space — **purged after 90 days idle** |

::: {.callout-warning}
**Talapas is NOT backed up.** You are responsible for your own backups. Keep large data in `/projects`; clean up `/scratch`.
:::

## Software: modules (Lmod)

Talapas software is loaded on demand with **Lmod** — per shell, so reload it in every session/job.

``` bash
module spider R          # search for software
module avail             # list loadable modules
module load R/4.4.1      # load a specific version (reproducible!)
module list              # what's loaded now
module purge             # unload everything
```

::: {.callout-note}
Always pin a version (`R/4.4.1`, not just `R`) so your analysis is reproducible later.
:::

## Partitions & SLURM

Jobs go to **partitions** (queues) via the **SLURM** scheduler. Every job must name its **`--account`** (your PIRG).

| Partition | Typical use | Max wall time |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|---------------|
| `compute` | Standard CPU jobs | 1 day |
| `computelong` | Long CPU jobs | 14 days |
| `gpu` / `gpulong` | GPU jobs (short / long) | 1 day / 14 d |
| `memory` / `memorylong` | High-memory CPU (up to 4 TB) | 1 day / 14 d |
| `interactive` / `interactivegpu` | Short interactive sessions | 12 h / 8 h |
| `preempt` | All nodes; may be preempted | Variable |

## Submitting work to SLURM

``` bash
# Batch job (the normal way to run real work)
sbatch my_script.sh

# Interactive session (testing / debugging)
srun --pty --partition=interactive --account=myPIRG \
     --time=2:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=8G /bin/bash

squeue -u $USER     # your jobs in the queue
scancel JOBID       # cancel a job
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Golden rule: **never run heavy computation on a login node.** Anything longer than a few seconds belongs in `srun` or `sbatch`.
:::

## Anatomy of a batch script

``` bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_analysis   # name
#SBATCH --partition=compute      # queue
#SBATCH --account=myPIRG         # your PIRG (required)
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00          # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4        # cores
#SBATCH --mem=16G                # memory
#SBATCH --output=out_%j.log      # %j = job ID

module load R/4.4.1              # load modules AFTER #SBATCH lines
Rscript my_analysis.R            # do the work
```

::: incremental
-   `#SBATCH` lines are scheduler directives, not run by bash.
-   Request only what you need — smaller jobs start sooner.
:::

# Working interactively {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## VS Code + Remote-SSH

::: incremental
-   **VS Code** is a free editor that can connect *into* Talapas over SSH.
-   Install the **Remote – SSH** and **Remote Explorer** extensions.
-   Add the host `login.talapas.uoregon.edu`, connect (password + Duo), and a green banner confirms you're on Talapas.
-   Browse remote files, edit scripts, and use the **integrated terminal** — all in one window.
-   The **Quarto extension** lets you edit and render `.qmd` documents right there.
:::

## Open OnDemand (browser, no SSH)

::: incremental
-   Web portal: [ondemand.talapas.uoregon.edu](https://ondemand.talapas.uoregon.edu) — Chrome or Firefox.
-   No SSH client needed; great for beginners.
-   File browser for uploads/downloads.
-   Launch **interactive apps**: JupyterLab, RStudio, MATLAB, remote desktop.
-   Easiest way to get an RStudio or Jupyter session on Talapas.
:::

# Reproducible environments {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why pin your environment?

::: incremental
-   So you can **reproduce a result six months later**.
-   So a co-author runs the **same package versions**.
-   So you avoid days of dependency debugging on Talapas.
-   Two layers cover most cases: **`renv`** (R packages) and **containers** (everything).
:::

## renv + containers (brief)

``` r
# renv: pin exact R-package versions (reads renv.lock)
install.packages("renv")
renv::restore()
```

``` bash
# Container: a self-contained image (R + Bioconductor + system deps)
# Laptop uses Docker; Talapas uses Apptainer (Docker isn't allowed there)
module load apptainer
apptainer pull docker://ghcr.io/wcresko/scrnaseq_tutorial:latest
apptainer exec scrnaseq_tutorial_latest.sif R
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Docker** on your laptop, **Apptainer** on Talapas — same image, reproducible either way.
:::

# Recap & what's next {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Recap

::: incremental
-   **CPU / RAM / disk** — RAM is usually the limiting resource for single-cell work.
-   The **OS** manages processes, memory, files, and security for you.
-   An **HPC cluster** = many nodes + shared storage + a scheduler; use it when your laptop runs out of room or time.
-   On **Talapas**: PIRG + account, SSH + Duo, mind your file systems, `module load`, and submit jobs with **SLURM** — never on the login node.
-   **VS Code / Open OnDemand** make remote work comfortable; **renv + containers** make it reproducible.
:::
